title: Gilt-Bronze Incense Burner of Baekje
creature: Bonghwang and Yong (Korean Phoenix and Dragon)
originLocation: Neungsan-ri Temple Site, Buyeo, South Chungcheong, Korea
medium: Cast gilt bronze
creator: Royal Baekje metalworkers
repository: Buyeo National Museum / National Museum of Korea
anatomy: sweeping crest feathers and arched tail plumes
magic pearl clasped beneath the phoenix chin
writhing dragon base supporting a lotus-and-mountain bowl
description: Excavated in 1993 from the muddy sluice pit of a royal temple workshop near Buyeo, this 62.5-centimeter gilt-bronze censer synthesizes Buddhist lotus cosmology with Daoist mountain immortality lore. At its apex perches a poised Bonghwang phoenix clutching a sacred cintamani pearl beneath its beak, while below, a dynamic single-horned Yong dragon coils upward from the circular foot to hold the mountain-tiered bowl in its jaws. Pierced smoke vents hidden among seventy-four miniature peaks and mythical beasts allowed rising incense to animate both celestial creatures in swirling vapor.

title: Azure Dragon of the East (Gangseo Great Tomb Mural)
originLocation: Gangseo Great Tomb (Gangseo Daemyo), Nampo, South Pyongan, Korea
medium: Mineral pigments on polished granite tomb wall
creator: Unknown Goguryeo court painter
repository: In situ, Gangseo Three Tombs (UNESCO World Heritage Site)
anatomy: sinuous scaled serpentine body banded in mineral blues, reds, and greens
swept-back horns and flaming shoulder wings
outstretched taloned legs striding through empty space
description: Painted directly onto the dressed granite slabs of the eastern burial chamber wall at Gangseo Daemyo without a plaster ground, this mural depicts Cheongnyong, the directional guardian of the East among the Four Symbols (Sasin). The dragon bounds forward with explosive linear energy, its slender neck arched in an S-curve and its jaws parted to exhale auspicious qi flames. Preserved in vivid malachite, cinnabar, and ink outlines, the creature guarded the royal occupant's afterlife realm against eastern malevolent spirits.

title: White Tiger of the West (Gangseo Great Tomb Mural)
originLocation: Gangseo Great Tomb (Gangseo Daemyo), Nampo, South Pyongan, Korea
medium: Mineral pigments on polished granite tomb wall
creator: Unknown Goguryeo court painter
repository: In situ, Gangseo Three Tombs (UNESCO World Heritage Site)
anatomy: elongated draconic torso striped in pale white and ink
feathered flame-wings sprouting from the shoulders
gaping fanged maw with protruding crimson tongue
description: Facing Cheongnyong from the western granite wall of the Gangseo Great Tomb, Baekho embodies the celestial guardian of the West, autumn, and martial metal in Goguryeo funerary cosmology. Rather than a naturalistic feline, the Goguryeo master conceived the White Tiger as a hybrid winged dragon-cat with a whip-thin serpentine spine, feathered forelimbs, and glaring eyes. Its ferocious roar and lunging stride mirror the Azure Dragon across the burial vault to establish a balanced cosmic axis around the stone coffin.

title: Black Tortoise of the North (Gangseo Great Tomb Mural)
originLocation: Gangseo Great Tomb (Gangseo Daemyo), Nampo, South Pyongan, Korea
medium: Mineral pigments on polished granite tomb wall
creator: Unknown Goguryeo court painter
repository: In situ, Gangseo Three Tombs (UNESCO World Heritage Site)
anatomy: hexagonal-plated tortoise carapace
coiling scaled serpent knotted tightly around the shell
confronting reptilian heads locked nose-to-nose
description: Occupying the rear northern wall of the Gangseo Great Tomb, this celebrated Goguryeo masterpiece portrays Hyeonmu, the guardian deity of the North, winter, and the watery underworld. A powerful long-necked tortoise and a muscular spotted serpent loop around one another in a figure-eight knot, twisting their necks backward to lock eyes in intense equilibrium. In East Asian yin-yang symbolism, their union fused terrestrial endurance and regenerative vitality at the threshold of death.

title: Vermilion Bird of the South (Gangseo Great Tomb Mural)
originLocation: Gangseo Great Tomb (Gangseo Daemyo), Nampo, South Pyongan, Korea
medium: Mineral pigments on polished granite tomb wall
creator: Unknown Goguryeo court painter
repository: In situ, Gangseo Three Tombs (UNESCO World Heritage Site)
anatomy: outspread crimson-tipped wings raised in heraldic display
curling ornamental head-crest
sweeping peacock-like tail plumes
description: Flanking the southern entrance passage of the Gangseo Great Tomb, Jujak—the Vermilion Bird of the South and solar fire—spreads its layered pinions to repel impurity from the threshold of the burial chamber. Unlike the terrestrial phoenix Bonghwang, which heralds peaceful rule, Jujak served specifically as a fierce astral sentinel of the southern sky quadrant. Cinnabar highlights and rhythmic calligraphic brushwork lend its fanned tail feathers the visual motion of rising flames.

title: Monster-Mask Ridge-End Tile (Gwimyeonwa)
originLocation: Former Gapsansa Temple Site, Gyeongju, North Gyeongsang, Korea
medium: Molded and carved gray earthenware
creator: Unknown Unified Silla tile workshop
repository: Tokyo National Museum
anatomy: bulging spherical eyes beneath knotted brows
bared fangs and flared leonine nostrils
foliate mane and horned brow ridge
description: Mounted at the exposed hip-ridge terminus of a Buddhist temple roof in royal Gyeongju, this high-relief earthenware tile confronts approaching storms and pestilential spirits with a ferocious monster countenance known in Korean tradition as gwimyeon and popularly linked to the dokkaebi goblin. Deeply undercut eyeballs, upturned tusks, and scrolling beard curls create dramatic chiaroscuro in sunlight while framing a central boss pierced for securing the tile to the wooden ridgepole. Unified Silla roof tiles transformed fierce demonic visages into benevolent architectural guardians of sacred space.

title: Celadon Ewer in the Shape of a Fish-Dragon
originLocation: Goryeo royal kilns (likely Gangjin, South Jeolla), Korea
medium: Stoneware with incised and carved decoration under celadon glaze, iron-brown eyes
creator: Unknown Goryeo master potter
repository: National Museum of Korea, Seoul (National Treasure No. 61)
anatomy: horned draconic head with upturned snout spout and fanged jaws
plump scaled carp torso with serrated pectoral fins
ascending tail fin rising above swirled lotus waves
description: Celebrated as a pinnacle of twelfth-century Goryeo sculptural celadon (sanghyeong cheongja), this ritual wine ewer captures the mythical Eoryong mid-metamorphosis as a carp leaps the Dragon Gate waterfall to become a celestial dragon. The creature's fierce dragon head, accented with underglaze iron-black pupils, forms the pouring spout, while its plump fish body rests upon stylized wave crests and a twisted lotus-stem handle arches behind its dorsal ridge. Translucent jade-green glaze pools into incised scales and fin rays, lending aquatic shimmer to the hybrid beast.

title: Shrine Guardian Lion-Dog (Komainu)
medium: Joined-block carved wood (yosegi-zukuri) with traces of pigment
creator: Unknown Heian Buddhist-Shinto sculptor
repository: Portland Art Museum, Oregon
anatomy: muscular seated leonine chest and braced forelegs
tightly curled mane locks cascading over the shoulders
snarling muzzle forming the cosmic syllable A or Un
description: Adapted from Tang- and Korean-transmitted guardian lions (hence the literal name 'Goguryeo dog'), wooden Komainu pairs stood inside covered Shinto shrine sanctuaries and imperial palace halls during the Heian period before outdoor stone examples became common. Carved from joined wood blocks, this twelfth-century guardian sits tautly upright with broad chest, bulging eyes, and stylized spiral curls worn smooth by centuries of incense and ritual veneration. Paired with an open-mouthed counterpart, the beast embodied the beginning and end of the cosmos while barring malevolent spirits from sacred thresholds.

title: Hell Wardens Tormenting Sinners (Jigoku Zōshi)
medium: Ink and color on paper handscroll (emakimono)
creator: Court atelier associated with Cloistered Emperor Go-Shirakawa
repository: Tokyo National Museum (National Treasure of Japan)
anatomy: towering crimson- and ochre-skinned muscular bodies
wild flame-like hair and glaring yellow eyes
loincloths of animal pelt and iron torture implements
description: Created for the treasury of Cloistered Emperor Go-Shirakawa during the turbulent twilight of the Heian court, the Jigoku Zōshi handscrolls offer some of the earliest surviving Japanese visual codifications of the Oni. In these harrowing scenes from the Sixteen Lesser Hells, giant red-skinned and beast-headed gokusotsu (hell wardens) tower over naked sinners amid swirling tongues of vermilion fire. Dynamic brushwork and grotesque anatomical exaggeration established the visual archetype of the horned, loincloth-clad Oni that dominated subsequent Japanese folklore.

title: Lantern-Bearing Demon Tentōki
originLocation: West Golden Hall, Kōfuku-ji, Nara, Japan
medium: Painted cypress wood (hinoki) with inlaid rock-crystal eyes (gyokugan)
creator: Kōben (third son of Unkei, Kei School)
repository: Kōfuku-ji National Treasure Hall, Nara (National Treasure of Japan)
anatomy: short forehead horns and fang-filled grimace
inlaid crystal eyes glaring upward from beneath furrowed brows
sinewy three-toed and three-fingered crimson body supporting a temple lantern
description: Sculpted in 1215 by Kei-school master Kōben as a companion to the dragon-wrapped Ryūtōki, this 77.8-centimeter wooden Oni subverts demonic terror with wry, muscular realism. Rather than being trampled underfoot by one of the Four Heavenly Kings, Tentōki has been converted to Buddhist service and stands on his own stocky legs, hoisting a heavy wooden lantern across his left shoulder to illuminate the Buddha's altar. Veined limbs, inlaid rock-crystal eyes, and a defiant upward scowl capture the comic strain of an unruly demon pressed into pious labor.

title: Artifact Spirits in the Night Parade of One Hundred Demons
medium: Ink and color on paper handscroll (emakimono)
creator: Traditionally attributed to Tosa Mitsunobu
repository: Shinju-an Subtemple, Daitoku-ji, Kyoto (Important Cultural Property)
anatomy: discarded straw sandals, parasols, staffs, and robes sprouting arms and legs
single glaring eyes and grinning mouths emerging from lacquered or woven surfaces
processional postures parodying court and monastic parades
description: Preserved at the Daitoku-ji subtemple of Shinju-an in Kyoto, this celebrated Muromachi handscroll is the foundational masterpiece of the Hyakki Yagyō ('Night Parade of One Hundred Demons') genre. Without explanatory text, a riotous nocturnal cavalcade of tsukumogami—household utensils, silk robes, parasols, and musical instruments that gained sentient spirits after a century of use—capers across the paper before fleeing the rising morning sun. Its inventive fusion of everyday material culture with monstrous limbs inspired centuries of Edo and modern yōkai imagery.

title: Golden Shachihoko Roof Finial of Nagoya Castle
originLocation: Nagoya Castle Main Keep, Owari Province (Nagoya), Japan
dateDisplay: 1612 CE (Keichō 17; pre-1945 archival photograph of original finial)
medium: Cypress wood core plated in hammered gold scales over copper-lead
creator: Commissioned by Tokugawa Ieyasu
repository: Formerly Nagoya Castle Tenshu (original destroyed in 1945 air raid)
anatomy: ferocious roaring tiger head with upturned fangs
overlapping gold-plated carp scales
vertical tail fin arched skyward to summon rain
description: Installed atop the main keep of Nagoya Castle in 1612 by order of shogun Tokugawa Ieyasu, this monumental 2.6-meter Kinshachi ('golden shachihoko') combined the head of a roaring tiger with the gleaming scaled body and skyward-flung tail of a carp. In Japanese castle architecture, the amphibious Shachihoko was believed to swallow vast quantities of water and spout rain clouds if fire broke out below, doubling as an apotropaic talisman and a dazzling emblem of Tokugawa wealth. This archival pre-1945 photograph records the original Edo-period sculpture encased in its historic anti-theft wire mesh prior to its wartime loss.

title: Wind God and Thunder God Screens (Fūjin Raijin-zu)
creature: Fūjin and Raijin (Elemental Demon-Kami of Wind and Thunder)
localName: 風神・雷神 (風神雷神図屏風)
medium: Ink, mineral pigments, and silver on gold-foiled paper; pair of two-panel folding screens (byōbu)
creator: Tawaraya Sōtatsu
repository: Kennin-ji, Kyoto (entrusted to Kyoto National Museum; National Treasure of Japan)
anatomy: horned oni-like visages in emerald green (Fūjin) and chalk white (Raijin)
two-clawed feet braced upon swirling dark storm clouds
billowing wind-bag and circular halo of taiko thunder drums
description: Hovering at the upper corners of an expansive ground of gleaming gold leaf, Tawaraya Sōtatsu's Fūjin and Raijin distill Japan's storm kami into exuberant, Oni-bodied elemental forces. On the right screen, green-skinned Fūjin hurtles into view clutching an inflated cloth sack of gale winds, while on the left, white-skinned Raijin balances amid dark tarashikomi ink clouds inside a ring of thunder drums. As the founding masterpiece of the Rinpa school, Sōtatsu's composition transformed fearsome tempest demons into vital, playful presences of nature.

title: White Porcelain Dragon Jar (Unryongmun Ho)
originLocation: Bunwon official kilns, Gwangju, Gyeonggi, Korea
medium: White porcelain painted in underglaze iron-brown oxide
creator: Unknown Joseon court potter
repository: National Museum of Korea, Seoul (Dongwon Collection)
anatomy: whiskered snout and branching antlers
undulating serpentine body swept in bold iron-oxide brushstrokes
clawed limbs striding across stylized cloud scrolls
description: When Hideyoshi's late-sixteenth-century invasions disrupted Joseon's imports of cobalt pigment for blue-and-white court wares, royal potters turned to native iron-oxide slip to paint auspicious dragons across milky baekja porcelain jars. Executed with swift, calligraphic freedom around the vessel's swelling shoulder, this Korean Yong darts through scrolling clouds with wind-blown mane and comic vitality rather than rigid imperial menace. Used at court banquets to hold wine or flowers, dragon jars invoked sovereign authority alongside life-giving rain for agriculture.

title: Kappa from the Illustrated Night Parade of a Hundred Demons
medium: Monochrome woodblock book illustration (ehon) on washi paper
creator: Toriyama Sekien
repository: Published in Gazu Hyakki Yagyō (multiple Edo editions preserved in public collections)
anatomy: water-filled cranial dish (sara) ringed by coarse fringe hair
ridged tortoise-like dorsal shell
webbed amphibious hands and feet
description: Emerging from a clump of riverbank lotus leaves in Toriyama Sekien's landmark 1776 yōkai compendium Gazu Hyakki Yagyō, the mischievous Kappa crouches with webbed hands and a watchful frog-like gaze. Sekien synthesized regional water-imp lore into a canonical anatomy featuring a scaly child-sized body, a turtle carapace, and the vital recessed dish (sara) atop its skull whose spilled water saps the creature's supernatural strength. Feared for luring horses and swimmers into rivers yet placated with cucumbers and polite bows, the Kappa became Japan's quintessential freshwater spirit.

title: Nekomata from the Illustrated Night Parade of a Hundred Demons
medium: Monochrome woodblock book illustration (ehon) on washi paper
creator: Toriyama Sekien
repository: Published in Gazu Hyakki Yagyō (multiple Edo editions preserved in public collections)
anatomy: bipedal domestic cat standing upright like a human
distinctive split or twin tail
shamisen-player kerchief and pawed kimono gestures
description: In Toriyama Sekien's Gazu Hyakki Yagyō, an aged domestic cat that has lived long enough for its tail to split in two rears onto its hind legs beside a folding screen and a discarded shamisen plectrum—a sly visual pun on geisha ('cat') culture and cat-skin shamisen lutes. Whereas medieval chronicles such as Fujiwara no Teika's Meigetsuki described mountain-dwelling Nekomata as dog-sized man-eating beasts, Edo urban print culture recast them as uncanny household shapeshifters capable of speech, necromancy, and nocturnal dance.

title: Tamamo-no-Mae and the Nine-Tailed Fox Spirit
localName: 玉藻前・九尾の狐 (今昔画図続百鬼)
medium: Monochrome woodblock book illustration (ehon) on washi paper
creator: Toriyama Sekien
repository: Published in Konjaku Gazu Zoku Hyakki (multiple Edo editions preserved in public collections)
anatomy: aristocratic Heian court lady enveloped by spectral mist
emergent fox visage with pointed ears and narrow snout
fan of nine plumed tails unfurling across the sky
description: Published in Sekien's 1779 sequel encyclopedia Konjaku Gazu Zoku Hyakki, this atmospheric woodcut captures the unmasking of Tamamo-no-Mae, the dazzling court favorite of twelfth-century Emperor Konoe who was exposed by court diviner Abe no Yasuchika as a millennia-old nine-tailed fox spirit. Sekien renders the courtesan in layered Heian robes while her true kyūbi no kitsune form—snarling muzzle and nine billowing tails—rises like smoke from her shoulders. According to legend, when hunted down on the Nasu plain, the slain fox petrified into the poisonous Killing Stone (Sesshō-seki).

title: Prophetic Ningyo Caught in Toyama Bay (Bunka 2 Kawaraban)
localName: 人魚 (越中国四方浦人魚之図)
medium: Woodblock-printed news broadside (kawaraban) with hand-applied color
creator: Anonymous Edo broadside publisher
repository: Tsubouchi Memorial Theatre Museum, Waseda University, Tokyo
anatomy: humanoid female head with flowing black hair and dual horns
colossal scaled carp torso bearing three circular flank eyes
webbed bird-like claws beneath the belly
description: Sold on city streets as an ephemeral kawaraban news sheet in the summer of 1805, this woodblock broadside reports a gigantic horned Ningyo allegedly netted off Etchū Province in Toyama Bay. Far removed from Western siren iconography, the Edo Ningyo merges a horned human visage with a massive carp body, three flank-mounted eyes, and clawed limbs. Its printed inscription promises that merely viewing an image of the prodigy confers longevity and wards off epidemic calamity—an auspicious visual talisman closely anticipating the later Amabie broadsides.

title: Baku, the Dream-Devouring Chimera
medium: Color woodblock print on paper
creator: Katsushika Hokusai
repository: Public collections (Edo woodblock impression)
anatomy: curling elephant trunk and curved ivory tusks
spotted leopard-like pelt and rhinoceros eyes
ox-like tail and clawed tiger paws
description: Katsushika Hokusai endows the benevolent Baku with coiled muscular torsion, combining an elephant's proboscis and tusks, a spotted feline coat, a flowing mane, and formidable tiger claws. Transmitted from Chinese protective beast lore into Japanese bedroom ritual, the Baku was invoked by sleepers waking from nightmares with the threefold plea 'Baku-san, come eat my dream.' Edo households placed Baku illustrations beneath pillows or carved its chimeric likeness onto temple crossbeams to consume malign portents and pestilence.

title: Hirado Porcelain Incense Burner in the Form of a Kirin
medium: Molded Hirado porcelain with underglaze cobalt blue and brown details
creator: Mikawachi porcelain workshop (Hirado Domain)
repository: Walters Art Museum, Baltimore
anatomy: single backward-swept horn crowning a draconic head
slender deer-like body and cloven hooves
curling shoulder flames and bushy upturned tail
description: Modeled in pure white Hirado porcelain at the domainal kilns of Mikawachi, this sculptural kōro (incense burner) portrays the auspicious Kirin seated haunches-down with its draconic head reared skyward to vent fragrant smoke through its parted jaws. Revered in East Asian cosmology as the noblest of beasts—so gentle that it refuses to tread upon living grass or insects—the Kirin manifests only during the reign of a virtuous sage. Crisp hand-carved flame scrolls and delicate cobalt-blue accents highlight the creature's single horn and supernatural poise.

title: The Earth Spider Generating Monsters at the Mansion of Lord Minamoto no Yorimitsu
creature: Tsuchigumo (Giant Demon Spider) and Hyakki Yōkai
localName: 土蜘蛛 (源頼光公館土蜘作妖怪図)
medium: Polychrome woodblock print triptych (ōban tate-e nishiki-e)
creator: Utagawa Kuniyoshi
repository: Tokyo National Museum / Victoria and Albert Museum (multiple impressions)
anatomy: bloated mottled arachnid body with glaring demon eyes
sticky silken web filaments cast over sleeping samurai
swarming army of horned, three-eyed, and tsukumogami specters
description: Published at the height of the austere Tenpō Reforms in 1843, Utagawa Kuniyoshi's celebrated triptych ostensibly depicts the tenth-century general Minamoto no Yorimitsu (Raikō) bedridden with fever as the monstrous Earth Spider (Tsuchigumo) looms above him, unleashing a swirling legion of ghouls behind his retainers' backs. Edo townspeople immediately read the composition as daring political satire against shogunal chief councilor Mizuno Tadakuni, identifying individual yōkai with censored professions and grievances. Despite authorities confiscating the woodblocks, pirate editions circulated widely across Edo.

title: Takiyasha the Witch and the Skeleton Spectre
localName: がしゃどくろ・骸骨の怪 (相馬の古内裏)
medium: Polychrome woodblock print triptych (ōban tate-e nishiki-e)
creator: Utagawa Kuniyoshi
repository: Victoria and Albert Museum, London / Honolulu Museum of Art
anatomy: gargantuan human skeleton spanning two full triptych sheets
anatomically detailed ribcage, clavicle, and articulated phalanges
hollow eye sockets looming through shredded bamboo palace blinds
description: Arguably the most iconic supernatural triptych in ukiyo-e history, Kuniyoshi's Sōma no furu-dairi condenses an army of spectral skeletons from Santō Kyōden's romance Utö Yasukata Chūgiden into a single monumental colossus tearing through the ruined Soma palace blinds to menace the warrior Ōya Tarō Mitsukuni. Drawing on imported Dutch anatomical engravings, Kuniyoshi rendered the towering ribcage and bony hands with startling osteological precision as Princess Takiyasha chants from a handscroll at left. In twentieth-century folklore revivals, Kuniyoshi's unnamed specter became the definitive visual model for the giant starving-dead yōkai Gashadokuro.

title: Higashimachi Festival Float Ceiling Painting: Phoenix (Hō-ō)
localName: 鳳凰 (東町祭屋台天井絵 鳳凰図)
medium: Mineral pigments, gold leaf, and animal-skin glue tempera on paulownia wood panel
creator: Katsushika Hokusai
repository: Hokusai-kan Museum, Obuse, Nagano
anatomy: fierce golden-eyed avian head crowned with jewel-like crests
iridescent wings layered in vermilion, azurite, malachite, and gold leaf
sinuous wheeling neck and peacock-eyed tail streamers
description: Painted by an eighty-five-year-old Katsushika Hokusai for the coffered ceiling of the Higashimachi neighborhood festival float in Obuse, this dazzling 126-centimeter square panel envelopes the viewer in the wheeling plumage of the sacred Hō-ō. Paired with a companion Dragon panel to represent cosmic yin and yang, the celestial bird coils across the paulownia frame in a vortex of cinnabar red, ultramarine, malachite green, and flecks of gold leaf. Hokusai gave the bird three-dimensional intensity so that revelers gazing upward beneath the moving float saw an auspicious omen of harmony blazing overhead.

title: Miyamoto Musashi Killing a Giant Nue (Mountain Beast)
medium: Polychrome woodblock print (ōban tate-e nishiki-e)
creator: Utagawa Kuniyoshi
repository: Public collections (Honchō Suikoden warrior series)
anatomy: snarling beast head with jagged fangs and flared nostrils
striped tiger-like limbs and razor claws
spined, chimeric mountain-monster torso pinned beneath the swordsman
description: From Kuniyoshi's kinetic warrior series Eight Hundred Heroes of Our Country's Suikoden, this vertical print pits the legendary swordsman Miyamoto Musashi astride a writhing mountain monster deep on the border of Echizen, Mino, and Hida provinces. While the cartouche calls the creature a 'mountain shark-fish' (yamazame), its striped tiger limbs, monstrous fanged head, and hybrid anatomy directly echo the classic Heike Monogatari iconography of the Nue—the night-crying chimera with a monkey's head, tanuki's body, tiger's legs, and snake's tail. Kuniyoshi fills almost the entire frame with the beast's contorted body to heighten the hero's perilous strike.

title: Appearance of the Prophetic Sea Spirit Amabie in Higo Province
localName: アマビエ (肥後国海中の怪)
medium: Woodblock-printed news broadside (kawaraban) on paper
creator: Anonymous Edo broadside woodcarver
repository: Kyoto University Main Library
anatomy: long streaming hair and bird-like beak
diamond-scaled torso from the neck down
three fin-like legs standing upright above ocean waves
description: Preserved in a single surviving Edo news broadside (kawaraban) at Kyoto University Library, this naïve yet unforgettable woodcut records a glowing marine spirit that emerged nightly from the sea off Higo Province in the fourth month of 1846. Addressing a local official who rowed out to investigate, the beaked, scaly, three-legged creature identified itself as Amabie, prophesied six years of bountiful harvests, and instructed people to copy and share its portrait should epidemic disease strike. Nearly two centuries later, this exact 1846 woodblock image achieved global renown as an emblem of protection against pestilence.

title: Dragon in Smoke Escaping from Mount Fuji (Fujigoshi Ryū-zu)
medium: Ink and light color on silk hanging scroll (kakemono)
creator: Katsushika Hokusai
repository: Hokusai-kan Museum, Obuse, Nagano
anatomy: slender black-scaled serpentine body twisting vertically through dark smoke
three-clawed taloned limbs typical of Japanese dragons
horned, whiskered head gazing skyward toward the heavens
description: Completed in the first month of 1849—less than four months before Katsushika Hokusai died at the age of eighty-eight—this poignant hanging scroll pairs the snow-draped cone of sacred Mount Fuji with a dark Ryū ascending on a column of black cloud and smoke. Unlike five-clawed Chinese imperial dragons, the Japanese dragon displays three razor-sharp talons per foot as its sinuous spine corkscrews toward heaven. Art historians widely interpret the ascending dragon leaving earthly Fuji behind as Hokusai's spiritual self-portrait at the threshold of artistic immortality.

title: True Depiction of the Kashima Keystone (Kashima Kanameishi Shinzu)
localName: 大鯰 (鹿島要石真図・鯰絵)
medium: Polychrome woodblock print (namazu-e)
creator: Anonymous Edo ukiyo-e artist
repository: International Research Center for Japanese Studies (Nichibunken), Kyoto
anatomy: colossal dark-skinned subterranean catfish body
long sensory barbels thrashing beneath the earth
broad flattened head pinned down by a sacred keystone and sword
description: Within days of the devastating Ansei Edo Earthquake of November 1855, hundreds of anonymous namazu-e ('catfish prints') flooded Edo streets as protective talismans and social commentary. Divided into upper and lower registers, this print shows pilgrims venerating the sacred foundation stone (kaname-ishi) at Kashima Shrine above ground while, beneath the earth, the thunder-and-sword deity Takemikazuchi subdues the thrashing giant Ōnamazu whose subterranean tremors toppled castles and storehouses. Buyers pasted such prints to house beams to appease the seismic beast and ward off aftershocks.

title: Stone Guardian Haetae of Gyeongbokgung Palace
originLocation: Gwanghwamun Gate, Gyeongbokgung Palace, Seoul, Korea
dateDisplay: c. 1867 CE (Reconstruction of Gyeongbokgung under King Gojong)
medium: Carved granite
creator: Yi Se-uk (royal master stonemason of the Joseon court)
repository: Gyeongbokgung Palace / Gwanghwamun Precinct, Seoul
anatomy: stocky lion-like body covered in carved fish-like scales
vestigial horn bud atop the crown and bell hung at the chest
curling eyebrow tufts, broad grin, and short feathered flank wings
description: Carved in local granite by royal master mason Yi Se-uk during Prince Regent Heungseon Daewongun's 1867 reconstruction of Gyeongbokgung Palace, this pair of Haetae (also called Haechi) originally stood before Gwanghwamun Gate beside the Office of the Inspector-General (Saheonbu). In Korean court tradition, the Haetae possessed an innate moral sense to gore corrupt officials while also swallowing destructive fire qi flowing from Mount Gwanaksan toward the wooden palace halls. Its charming rounded muzzle, scalloped body scales, and ornamental chest bell became enduring emblems of Seoul.

title: Sōjōbō Instructs Young Yoshitsune in the Sword
localName: 大天狗・鞍馬山僧正坊
medium: Polychrome woodblock print diptych (ōban tate-e nishiki-e)
creator: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi
repository: National Gallery of Victoria, Melbourne / Los Angeles County Museum of Art
anatomy: flowing white mane, beard, and stern avian-inflected ascetic visage
yamabushi mountain-priest robes with miniature tokin pillbox cap
feathered tengu fan (ha-uchiwa) and attendant crow-tengu acolytes
description: Set amid nocturnal mists on sacred Mount Kurama north of Kyoto, Tsukioka Yoshitoshi's dramatic Meiji diptych portrays Sōjōbō, the immortal white-haired King of the Tengu, imparting secret swordsmanship to the exiled boy Minamoto no Yoshitsune (Ushiwakamaru). Wearing the pom-pommed cords and tiny black tokin cap of a Shugendō mountain ascetic while wielding a magical feathered fan, Sōjōbō embodies the mature daitengu ('greater tengu') alongside agile lesser tengu sparring in the pines. Yoshitoshi's crisp Meiji linework captures the uncanny dignity of Japan's martial mountain spirits.

title: Kiyohime Changing into a Serpent at Hidaka River
localName: 清姫 (新形三十六怪撰 清姫日高川に蛇躰と成るの図)

creator: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi

anatomy: coiling scaled serpent tail emerging from soaked, scale-patterned kimono
pale demonic visage with wild streaming hair drenched in rain
draconic claws gripping the stone stairs above the Hidaka River
description: Created for Tsukioka Yoshitoshi's final masterwork series New Forms of Thirty-Six Ghosts (Shinkei Sanjūrokkaisen), this haunting vertical print illustrates the climax of the Dōjō-ji legend, in which the spurned maiden Kiyohime's consuming rage transforms her into a fire-breathing dragon-serpent as she swims the flooded Hidaka River after the monk Anchin. Yoshitoshi subtly fuses woman and reptile: her drenched blue robe clings like fish scales to her limbs while a sinuous serpent tail coils up the stone embankment behind her. Slanted silver-gray rain lines heighten the psychological intensity of late Meiji supernatural printmaking.
